messages: I’m using the statistical-analysis skill because this request calls for a Welch comparison, diagnostics, a plot, and reproducible R code. I’ll keep all reads and outputs confined to this workspace.

The file has 24 complete rows: 12 participants in A and 12 in B, with one numeric outcome per participant and unique-looking IDs. I’ll use the prespecified Welch method, while checking missingness, group support, variance imbalance, distribution shape, and sensitivity to single observations.

Group B averaged **3.83 points higher** than group A. The **95% Welch confidence interval was 2.30 to 5.36 points** (A: mean 10.17, SD 1.75; B: mean 14.00, SD 1.86; 12 participants per group).

| Result | n | Mean (SD), points | B − A (95% CI) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Group A | 12 | 10.17 (1.75) | — |
| Group B | 12 | 14.00 (1.86) | — |
| Mean difference | 24 | — | 3.83 (2.30 to 5.36) |

Practically, the observed participants in B scored about four points higher on average. The interval suggests that, under the sampling and independence assumptions, the population mean difference could reasonably be roughly 2.3–5.4 points. Whether that is substantively important depends on the scale and a practical importance threshold, neither of which was supplied.

Diagnostics found no missing data or duplicate participant IDs. Group variances were similar (variance ratio 1.13), Q–Q plots showed no conspicuous departures from normality, and leave-one-participant-out estimates ranged from 3.55 to 4.11 points. With only 12 observations per group, however, tail behavior remains difficult to assess.

This is an unadjusted observational association—not a causal effect. Confounding, selection, or differences in group composition may explain some or all of the difference. Independence was supplied by the study description but cannot be verified from the data, and generalizability depends on the unspecified sampling process.
